item.research_question: Can a single programmable nanoparticle conversion pathway, based on the thermal transformation of colloidal core-shell precursors, be used to synthesize all major types of polyelemental nanoparticles (high entropy alloys, high entropy intermetallics, and multiphase Janus structures) by varying stoichiometry and metal identity?
item.material_system: AuCu@PtPdM core-shell nanoparticles (where M = Ni or Fe); specifically Au2Cu@PdPtNi, AuCu2@PdPtNi, AuCu@PtPdFe, and AuCu@PdPtNi precursors converted into AurichCuPd-PtNi, AuCurichPd-PtNi, AuCuPtPdFe, and AuCuPdPtNi products.
item.processing_route: Colloidal synthesis of core-shell precursors followed by thermal annealing under forming gas at 800 °C for 2 hours; temperature variations of 600 °C (1 h) and 400 °C (1 h) were also used for catalyst testing.
item.test_conditions: Annealing at 800 °C, 600 °C, and 400 °C under forming gas; electrochemical testing in 1 M KOH aqueous solution for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) using a three-electrode system.
key_findings: Annealing nonequimolar Au2Cu@PdPtNi precursors (10.1 ± 1.2 nm) yielded monodisperse Janus AurichCuPd-PtNi NPs with an average diameter of 9.2 ± 1.0 nm.
Annealing nonequimolar AuCu2@PdPtNi precursors (12.7 ± 1.3 nm) yielded monodisperse Janus AuCurichPd-PtNi NPs with an average diameter of 11.2 ± 1.8 nm.
Annealing equimolar AuCu@PtPdFe precursors resulted in single-phase High Entropy Intermetallic (HEI) AuCuPtPdFe NPs (10.3 ± 0.9 nm) with L10 fct-PtFe and L12-Pt3Fe structures.
Annealing equimolar AuCu@PdPtNi precursors predominantly yielded High Entropy Alloy (HEA) NPs (53% fcc phase) with homogeneous mixing, alongside 26% intermediate and 21% Janus-like particles.
The HEI_800/C catalyst (annealed at 800 °C) required an overpotential of only -0.128 V to reach 10 mA cm−2, significantly lower than HEI_400/C (-0.363 V) and commercial Pt/C (-0.243 V).
The mass activity of HEI_800/C NPs reached 26.82 A mgPt+Pd−1, which is 2.5 times higher than that of commercial Pt/C catalysts.
Atomistic simulations confirmed that Pt-Ni and Pt-Fe bonds are the strongest, driving the segregation of Pt with Ni or Fe to form Janus structures in nonequimolar systems.
Simulations indicated that Janus-like configurations appear at 900 K for 8 nm NPs but require 1300 K for 16 nm NPs, attributing this to surface relaxation and mechanical anisotropy.
item.mechanism: The final mixing states are governed by the balance between the enthalpy of mixing (ΔH mix) and the entropy of mixing (ΔS mix); nonequimolar stoichiometries lower ΔS mix, allowing positive ΔH mix to drive phase segregation (Janus), while equimolar stoichiometries maximize ΔS mix to favor single-phase alloys or intermetallics depending on specific bond enthalpies (e.g., Pt-Fe favors intermetallics).
item.limitations: Predicting specific phases a priori is difficult due to the many bonding interactions; simulations in a vacuum do not fully account for embedding environments in real experiments; intraparticle heterogeneity is challenging to detect experimentally; surface relaxation-induced segregation may prevent simulations from unequivocally supporting HEI or HEA formation.
item.future_work: Computational screening can be leveraged in the future to predict the final thermodynamic phases of PE NPs when constructing precursor core-shell NPs with specific metal identities and ratios.
quotes: Through systematic variations in stoichiometry and metal identity to the core‐shell precursor NPs, along with atomistic simulations that probe phase stabilities, we deduce that the final mixing states of the various NPs are governed by the balance between the enthalpy and entropy of mixing.
Annealing nonequimolar core‐shell AuxCu1‐x@PtPdM (M = Ni or Fe) NPs leads to the formation of AuCuPd‐PtM (M = Ni, Fe) Janus NPs.
